title: PulseQuilt load catalog — quick bench log
content:
Objective:
Run a set of quick exploratory benches for a mixed arrival pattern I’m calling "PulseQuilt" — alternating short, high-intensity pulses on top of a low steady background. Goal is to understand: how the runtime’s dynamic batching + KV cache behave when pulses land on partially warmed caches and how tail latency (p95/p99) responds to pulse frequency and magnitude.

Motivation / why this differs from previous: 
- Most microburst tests were pure spikes or Poisson arrivals. PulseQuilt mixes spike trains with a persistent low-rate baseline to emulate real client blends (chatty UI + occasional batch analytics).
- Hypothesis: prefix cache fragmentation across pulses will create mid-tail latency modes (not just cold vs hot).

Environment / config:
- Model: open-quant-gptj-6B-8bit (serving variant: gptj-6b-q8v2)
- Hardware: 4x A100-40GB equivalent (dedicated pod), single GPU per worker in this run
- Runtime: serving-runtime v3.7.1 (dynamic-batching=on, prefill_strategy=eager, kv_cache=true, cache_ttl=600s)
- Client harness: local runner (rust) that supports scripted arrival patterns, uses multiplexed HTTP/2 streaming
- Metrics capture: prometheus + local capture of per-request trace (latency_ms, cache_hit boolean, batch_size)

PulseQuilt definition used here:
- Background QPS: 2 rps (steady single-token-ish chat requests)
- Pulse: 600ms window, 120 rps within window, repeated every 8s (duty cycle ~7.5%)
- Pulse composition: 70% short (avg tokens 40) vs 30% long (avg tokens 320)
- Duration: 20 minutes per run (warmup 3 mins)

Key knobs varied across runs:
- batch_max_tokens: 2048 vs 4096
- batching_timeout_ms: 8, 20, 40
- cache_ttl: 60s vs 600s (to force faster eviction)
- enable_prefill_compaction: true/false (experimental flag)

Raw observations (high level):
- Warmup (first 3 min) consistent: cache hit-rate climbs to ~82% for short prefixes, long requests mostly miss prefill cache as expected.
- When pulse arrives: average batch size increases (expected) but variance in batch size spikes, which correlates strongly with p95 latency spikes.
- With batching_timeout_ms=8: p50 ~ 22ms, p95 ~ 210ms, p99 ~ 540ms in pulse windows (long-request fraction dominated tail).
- With batching_timeout_ms=40: p50 ~ 28ms, p95 ~ 300ms, p99 ~ 720ms but overall throughput higher (~+7%). Tradeoff: higher batching_timeout reduces tokens/sec cost but raises worst tail when pulses have many long requests.
- cache_ttl=60s: ligand for fragmentation — observed repeated small pulses evict/overwrite parts of the KV cache leading to cache churn; hit rate drops to ~60% mid-run and p99 jumps ~+30%.
- enable_prefill_compaction=true: reduced tail by ~8–12% in several runs; seems to help when mixed short/long requests hit the same worker because compaction reduces prefill amplification.

Representative numbers (single-run sample; pulse windows only):
- baseline (timeout=20, ttl=600, compaction=off): tokens/sec ~ 9.2k, p50=25ms, p95=260ms, p99=610ms, cache_hit=78%
- aggressive batching (timeout=40, ttl=600, compaction=on): tokens/sec ~ 9.9k, p50=32ms, p95=280ms, p99=550ms, cache_hit=80%
- low-ttl (timeout=20, ttl=60, compaction=off): tokens/sec ~ 8.6k, p50=27ms, p95=390ms, p99=860ms, cache_hit=61%

Quick ASCII heatmap sketch (pulse timeline; each char approx 1s):
- S = steady 2 rps, P = pulse high qps
SSSSS SSSSS PPPPPP SSSSSSS PPPPPP SSSSSS PPPPPP

Latency summary (pulse windows only):
- Two modal tail: 1) short-request dominated batches (good cache) -> p95 ~ 160–300ms; 2) long-request dominated batches (cold prefill) -> p95 ~ 350–900ms.
- The mixed nature creates an intermediate worst-case when a long request lands at the end of a packed batch (batching timeout forces prefill + decode overlap) — this is where p99 suffers most.

Trace hits / examples (anecdotal):
- trace#1001: pulse start, batch size=27, one long request (320 tokens) + 26 short; worker created batch prefill for long req, short ones served from cache -> p99 for short reqs ~ 120ms but long req ~ 1.1s.
- trace#1156: compaction=true run, similar batch size=31, compaction reduced duplicated prefill work, long req dropped to 760ms.

Immediate conclusions / heuristics:
- For pulse-like patterns, small batching_timeout (~<=10ms) reduces p99 for short requests but starves throughput and increases cost. Use if p99 SLO is strict and request lengths skew short.
- Prefill compaction is promising — gives tail reduction without paying heavy throughput tax; worth enabling as a default for mixed workloads and validating on more seeds.
- Short cache_ttl amplifies tail risk in pulse patterns. Default production ttl should be conservative (>300s) unless memory pressure mandates otherwise.
- Consider segregating short vs long request paths (auto route by token-estimate) so long tokens go to a slower lane or dedicated workers during pulses. This avoids single batches being dominated by one long request.

Next steps / follow-ups:
- Run 5-seed experiment with compaction on/off, across two models (gptj-6b-q8v2 and llama-7b-q4). Capture deterministic traces for top 1% slowest with full decoded token counts. (JIRA: PERF-342 follow-up)
- Add an ingress classifier that pre-samples first 5 tokens to estimate length then steer to long/short lanes; bench impact on p99 and cost per token.
- Simulate higher duty cycles (20% pulses every 4s) to see saturation dynamics and check autoscaler reaction.
- Share compacted trace examples with runtime kernel team (link PR above) — ask if kernel-level prefill dedupe could be improved.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Save prometheus snapshots and raw traces to /tmp/pulsequilt-20250212 (done).
- Annotate run IDs in a follow-up doc and upload to Confluence.
- Reach out to Jun about running same pattern on Dedicated pool vs Private to test network/noise differences.

Oddities / open questions:
- Why did one run show p99 drop when compaction disabled? Hypothesis: lucky alignment of pulses with a hot cache on that exact worker — need more seeds to rule out noise.
- Is there an interaction between prefill_strategy=eager and dynamic-batching that causes prefetch thrashing for certain token distributions? Trace look needed.

If anybody reading: feel free to ping me (amar) for the raw traces. This is a working scrap — trying to capture the intuition and knobs before I forget.

End of PulseQuilt quick log.
